quotes.text: "Why so?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Why shouldn't my permission be

asked?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"What do you know about Lucy or girls or anything? What ever did you

say?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I said to Cecil, 'Take her or leave her; it's no business of mine!'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What a helpful answer!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The bother is this,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Freddy, you must come. There they still are!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I don't see you ought to go peeping like that."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Peeping like that! Can't I look out of my own window?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Still page 322?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The bother is this: I have put my foot in it with Cecil most awfully."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Not content with 'permission', which I did

give--that is to say, I said, 'I don't mind'--well, not content with

that, he wanted to know whether I wasn't off my head with joy. He

practically put it like this: Wasn't it a splendid thing for Lucy and

for Windy Corner generally if he married her? And he would have an

answer--he said it would strengthen his hand."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I hope you gave a careful answer, dear."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I answered 'No'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"There! Fly into a

stew! I can't help it--had to say it. I had to say no. He ought never to

have asked me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ridiculous child!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You think you're so holy and

truthful, but really it's only abominable conceit. Do you suppose that

a man like Cecil would take the slightest notice of anything you say? I

hope he boxed your ears. How dare you say no?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, do keep quiet, mother! I had to say no when I couldn't say yes. I

tried to laugh as if I didn't mean what I said, and, as Cecil laughed

too, and went away, it may be all right. But I feel my foot's in it. Oh,

do keep quiet, though, and let a man do some work."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I shall not keep quiet. You know all that has passed between

them in Rome; you know why he is down here, and yet you deliberately

insult him, and try to turn him out of my house."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not a bit!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I only let out I didn't like him. I don't hate

him, but I don't like him. What I mind is that he'll tell Lucy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, I like him,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I know his mother; he's

good, he's clever, he's rich, he's well connected--Oh, you needn't kick

the piano! He's well connected--I'll say it again if you like: he's

well connected."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And he has beautiful manners."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I liked him till just now. I suppose it's having him spoiling Lucy's

first week at home; and it's also something that Mr. Beebe said, not

knowing."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mr. Beebe?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't

see how Mr. Beebe comes in."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You know Mr. Beebe's funny way, when you never quite know what he

means. He said: 'Mr. Vyse is an ideal bachelor.' I was very cute, I

asked him what he meant. He said 'Oh, he's like me--better detached.' I

couldn't make him say any more, but it set me thinking. Since Cecil has

come after Lucy he hasn't been so pleasant, at least--I can't explain."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You never can, dear. But I can. You are jealous of Cecil because he may

stop Lucy knitting you silk ties."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Will this do?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"'Dear Mrs. Vyse,--Cecil has just

asked my permission about it, and I should be delighted if Lucy wishes

it.' Then I put in at the top, 'and I have told Lucy so.' I must write

the letter out again--'and I have told Lucy so. But Lucy seems very

uncertain, and in these days young people must decide for themselves.' I

said that because I didn't want Mrs. Vyse to think us old-fashioned. She

goes in for lectures and improving her mind, and all the time a thick

layer of flue under the beds, and the maid's dirty thumb-marks where you

turn on the electric light. She keeps that flat abominably--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Suppose Lucy marries Cecil, would she live in a flat, or in the

country?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Don't interrupt so foolishly. Where was I? Oh yes--'Young people must

decide for themselves. I know that Lucy likes your son, because she

tells me everything, and she wrote to me from Rome when he asked her

first.' No, I'll cross that last bit out--it looks patronizing. I'll

stop at 'because she tells me everything.' Or shall I cross that out,

too?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cross it out, too,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Then the whole thing runs: 'Dear Mrs. Vyse.--Cecil has just asked my

permission about it, and I should be delighted if Lucy wishes it, and

I have told Lucy so. But Lucy seems very uncertain, and in these days

young people must decide for themselves. I know that Lucy likes your

son, because she tells me everything. But I do not know--'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Look out!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Cecil!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "oh, Cecil, do tell me!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I promessi sposi,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She has accepted me,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am so glad,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Welcome as one of the family!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"This is indeed a joyous day! I feel sure that you

will make our dear Lucy happy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I hope so,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We mothers--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I say, Lucy!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Steady on!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not a kiss for me?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Would you take them into the garden and tell Mrs. Honeychurch all about

it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And I'd stop here and tell my mother."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We go with Lucy?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, you go with Lucy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "story."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Dear Mrs. Vyse,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is only a boy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I represent all

that he despises. Why should he want me for a brother-in-law?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mr. Beebe!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I've come for tea, Mr. Vyse. Do you suppose that I shall get it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I should say so. Food is the thing one does get here--Don't sit in that

chair; young Honeychurch has left a bone in it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Pfui!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I know,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I know. I can't think why Mrs. Honeychurch allows

it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I've come for tea and for gossip. Isn't this news?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "News? I don't understand you,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "News?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I met Sir Harry Otway as I came up; I have every reason to hope that I

am first in the field. He has bought Cissie and Albert from Mr. Flack!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Has he indeed?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Unpardonable question! To have stopped a week at Windy Corner and not

to have met Cissie and Albert, the semi-detached villas that have been

run up opposite the church! I'll set Mrs. Honeychurch after you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I'm shockingly stupid over local affairs,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I can't even remember the difference between a Parish

Council and a Local Government Board. Perhaps there is no difference, or

perhaps those aren't the right names. I only go into the country to see

my friends and to enjoy the scenery. It is very remiss of me. Italy and

London are the only places where I don't feel to exist on sufferance."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Let me see, Mr. Vyse--I forget--what is your profession?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have no profession,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It is another example of my

decadence. My attitude quite an indefensible one--is that so long as I

am no trouble to any one I have a right to do as I like. I know I ought

to be getting money out of people, or devoting myself to things I don't

care a straw about, but somehow, I've not been able to begin."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are very fortunate,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It is a wonderful

opportunity, the possession of leisure."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I am glad that you approve. I daren't face the healthy person--for

example, Freddy Honeychurch."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Freddy's a good sort, isn't he?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Admirable. The sort who has made England what she is."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Where are the others?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I insist on extracting

tea before evening service."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I suppose Anne never told them you were here. In this house one is so

coached in the servants the day one arrives. The fault of Anne is

that she begs your pardon when she hears you perfectly, and kicks the

chair-legs with her feet. The faults of Mary--I forget the faults of

Mary, but they are very grave. Shall we look in the garden?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I know the faults of Mary. She leaves the dust-pans standing on the

stairs."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"The fault of Euphemia is that she will not, simply will not, chop the

suet sufficiently small."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The faults of Freddy--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Ah, he has too many. No one but his mother can remember the faults of

Freddy. Try the faults of Miss Honeychurch; they are not innumerable."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She has none,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I quite agree. At present she has none."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "At present?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I'm not cynical. I'm only thinking of my pet theory about Miss

Honeychurch. Does it seem reasonable that she should play so

wonderfully, and live so quietly? I suspect that one day she will be

wonderful in both. The water-tight compartments in her will break down,

and music and life will mingle. Then we shall have her heroically good,

heroically bad--too heroic, perhaps, to be good or bad."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And at present you think her not wonderful as far as life goes?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Well, I must say I've only seen her at Tunbridge Wells, where she was

not wonderful, and at Florence. Since I came to Summer Street she has

been away. You saw her, didn't you, at Rome and in the Alps. Oh, I

forgot; of course, you knew her before. No, she wasn't wonderful in

Florence either, but I kept on expecting that she would be."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In what way?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I could as easily tell you what tune she'll play next. There was simply

the sense that she had found wings, and meant to use them. I can show

you a beautiful picture in my Italian diary: Miss Honeychurch as a

kite, Miss Bartlett holding the string. Picture number two: the string

breaks."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But the string never broke?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No. I mightn't have seen Miss Honeychurch rise, but I should certainly

have heard Miss Bartlett fall."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It has broken now,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Broken? What do you mean?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I meant,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that she is going to marry me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I am sorry; I must apologize. I had no idea you were intimate with her,

or I should never have talked in this flippant, superficial way. Mr.

Vyse, you ought to have stopped me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am sorry I have given you a shock,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I fear that

Lucy's choice does not meet with your approval."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Not that. But you ought to have stopped me. I know Miss Honeychurch

only a little as time goes. Perhaps I oughtn't to have discussed her so

freely with any one; certainly not with you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are conscious of having said something indiscreet?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No, I have said nothing indiscreet. I foresaw at Florence that her

quiet, uneventful childhood must end, and it has ended. I realized dimly

enough that she might take some momentous step. She has taken it. She

has learnt--you will let me talk freely, as I have begun freely--she has

learnt what it is to love: the greatest lesson, some people will tell

you, that our earthly life provides."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"She has

learnt through you,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"let it be your care that her knowledge is profitable to

her."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Grazie tante!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Have you heard?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Mr. Beebe, have you heard the news?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Indeed I have!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Mrs. Honeychurch, I'm going to do what I am always supposed to do, but

generally I'm too shy. I want to invoke every kind of blessing on

them, grave and gay, great and small. I want them all their lives to be

supremely good and supremely happy as husband and wife, as father and

mother. And now I want my tea."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You only asked for it just in time,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"How dare you

be serious at Windy Corner?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Fiasco"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you go to much of this sort of thing?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, now and then,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is it typical of country society?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I suppose so. Mother, would it be?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Plenty of society,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To me it seemed perfectly appalling, disastrous, portentous."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am so sorry that you were stranded."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Not that, but the congratulations. It is so disgusting, the way an

engagement is regarded as public property--a kind of waste place where

every outsider may shoot his vulgar sentiment. All those old women

smirking!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"One has to go through it, I suppose. They won't notice us so much next

time."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"But my point is that their whole attitude is wrong. An

engagement--horrid word in the first place--is a private matter, and

should be treated as such."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How tiresome!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Couldn't you have escaped to tennis?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't play tennis--at least, not in public. The neighbourhood is

deprived of the romance of me being athletic. Such romance as I have is

that of the Inglese Italianato."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Inglese Italianato?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "E un diavolo incarnato! You know the proverb?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I cannot help it if they do disapprove of me. There

are certain irremovable barriers between myself and them, and I must

accept them."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We all have our limitations, I suppose,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Sometimes they are forced on us, though,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It makes a difference doesn't it, whether we fully fence ourselves in,

or whether we are fenced out by the barriers of others?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Difference?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't see any

difference. Fences are fences, especially when they are in the same

place."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We were speaking of motives,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My dear Cecil, look here."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"This is me. That's Windy Corner. The rest of the

pattern is the other people. Motives are all very well, but the fence

comes here."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We weren't talking of real fences,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, I see, dear--poetry."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I tell you who has no 'fences,' as you call them,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"and

that's Mr. Beebe."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A parson fenceless would mean a parson defenceless."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't you like Mr. Beebe?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I never said so!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I consider him far above the average. I

only denied--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Now, a clergyman that I do hate,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"a clergyman that does have fences, and the most dreadful

ones, is Mr. Eager, the English chaplain at Florence. He was truly

insincere--not merely the manner unfortunate. He was a snob, and so

conceited, and he did say such unkind things."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What sort of things?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"There was an old man at the Bertolini whom he said had murdered his

wife."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps he had."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why 'no'?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He was such a nice old man, I'm sure."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Well, I did try to sift the thing. Mr. Eager would never come to the

point. He prefers it vague--said the old man had 'practically' murdered

his wife--had murdered her in the sight of God."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hush, dear!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"But isn't it intolerable

that a person whom we're told to imitate should go round spreading

slander? It was, I believe, chiefly owing to him that the old man was

dropped. People pretended he was vulgar, but he certainly wasn't that."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Poor old man! What was his name?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Harris,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Let's hope that Mrs. Harris there warn't no sich person,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Isn't Mr. Eager a parson of the cultured type?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't know. I hate him. I've heard him lecture on Giotto. I hate him.

Nothing can hide a petty nature. I HATE him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My goodness gracious me, child!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You'll blow

my head off! Whatever is there to shout over? I forbid you and Cecil to

hate any more clergymen."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I count myself a lucky person,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"When I'm in London I

feel I could never live out of it. When I'm in the country I feel the

same about the country. After all, I do believe that birds and trees and

the sky are the most wonderful things in life, and that the people who

live amongst them must be the best. It's true that in nine cases out of

ten they don't seem to notice anything. The country gentleman and

the country labourer are each in their way the most depressing of

companions. Yet they may have a tacit sympathy with the workings

of Nature which is denied to us of the town. Do you feel that, Mrs.

Honeychurch?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "'Come down, O maid, from yonder mountain height,'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What height?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"'Come down, O maid, from yonder mountain height, What pleasure lives

in height (the shepherd sang). In height and in the splendour of the

hills?' Let us take Mrs. Honeychurch's advice and hate clergymen no

more. What's this place?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Summer Street, of course,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cissie"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Albert"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Albert"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cissie"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The place is ruined!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Summer Street will

never be the same again."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cissie's"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Stop!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Here's Sir Harry. Now we shall know. Sir Harry, pull those things down

at once!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Mrs. Honeychurch, I meant to. I can't, I really can't turn out

Miss Flack."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Am I not always right? She ought to have gone before the contract was

signed. Does she still live rent free, as she did in her nephew's time?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But what can I do?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"An old lady, so very vulgar,

and almost bedridden."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Turn her out,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"and

all the capitals different--one with dragons in the foliage, another

approaching to the Ionian style, another introducing Mrs. Flack's

initials--every one different."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cissie"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The rent is absurdly low,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"and perhaps I am an easy

landlord. But it is such an awkward size. It is too large for the

peasant class and too small for any one the least like ourselves."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You ought to find a tenant at once,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It would be

a perfect paradise for a bank clerk."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Exactly!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"That is exactly what I fear, Mr.

Vyse. It will attract the wrong type of people. The train service has

improved--a fatal improvement, to my mind. And what are five miles from

a station in these days of bicycles?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Rather a strenuous clerk it would be,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Sir Harry!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I have an idea. How would you like

spinsters?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My dear Lucy, it would be splendid. Do you know any such?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes; I met them abroad."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Gentlewomen?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Yes, indeed, and at the present moment homeless. I heard from them last

week--Miss Teresa and Miss Catharine Alan. I'm really not joking. They

are quite the right people. Mr. Beebe knows them, too. May I tell them

to write to you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Indeed you may!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Here we are with the difficulty solved

already. How delightful it is! Extra facilities--please tell them they

shall have extra facilities, for I shall have no agents' fees. Oh,

the agents! The appalling people they have sent me! One woman, when

I wrote--a tactful letter, you know--asking her to explain her social

position to me, replied that she would pay the rent in advance. As

if one cares about that! And several references I took up were most

unsatisfactory--people swindlers, or not respectable. And oh, the

deceit! I have seen a good deal of the seamy side this last week. The

deceit of the most promising people. My dear Lucy, the deceit!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My advice,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"is to have nothing to do with

Lucy and her decayed gentlewomen at all. I know the type. Preserve me

from people who have seen better days, and bring heirlooms with them

that make the house smell stuffy. It's a sad thing, but I'd far rather

let to some one who is going up in the world than to some one who has

come down."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I think I follow you,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"but it is, as you say, a very

sad thing."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The Misses Alan aren't that!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, they are,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I haven't met them but I should say they

were a highly unsuitable addition to the neighbourhood."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't listen to him, Sir Harry--he's tiresome."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's I who am tiresome,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I oughtn't to come with my

troubles to young people. But really I am so worried, and Lady Otway

will only say that I cannot be too careful, which is quite true, but no

real help."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then may I write to my Misses Alan?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Please!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Beware! They are certain to have canaries. Sir Harry, beware of

canaries: they spit the seed out through the bars of the cages and then

the mice come. Beware of women altogether. Only let to a man."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Really--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Men don't gossip over tea-cups. If they get drunk, there's an end of

them--they lie down comfortably and sleep it off. If they're vulgar,

they somehow keep it to themselves. It doesn't spread so. Give me a

man--of course, provided he's clean."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cissie"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mrs. Honeychurch,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "what if we two walk home and leave you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Certainly!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Aha! young people, young people!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hopeless vulgarian!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Cecil!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I can't help it. It would be wrong not to loathe that man."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He isn't clever, but really he is nice."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No, Lucy, he stands for all that is bad in country life. In London he

would keep his place. He would belong to a brainless club, and his wife

would give brainless dinner parties. But down here he acts the little

god with his gentility, and his patronage, and his sham aesthetics, and

every one--even your mother--is taken in."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "All that you say is quite true,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wonder whether--whether it matters so very much."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It matters supremely. Sir Harry is the essence of that garden-party.

Oh, goodness, how cross I feel! How I do hope he'll get some vulgar

tenant in that villa--some woman so really vulgar that he'll notice

it. GENTLEFOLKS! Ugh! with his bald head and retreating chin! But let's

forget him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It would be wrong not to loathe Freddy"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Which way shall we go?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Are there two ways?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps the road is more sensible, as we're got up smart."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I'd rather go through the wood,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Why is it,

Lucy, that you always say the road? Do you know that you have never once

been with me in the fields or the wood since we were engaged?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Haven't I? The wood, then,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I had got an idea--I dare say wrongly--that you feel more at home with

me in a room."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A room?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Yes. Or, at the most, in a garden, or on a road. Never in the real

country like this."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, Cecil, whatever do you mean? I have never felt anything of the

sort. You talk as if I was a kind of poetess sort of person."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't know that you aren't. I connect you with a view--a certain type

of view. Why shouldn't you connect me with a room?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Do you know that you're right? I do. I must be a poetess after all.

When I think of you it's always as in a room. How funny!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A drawing-room, pray? With no view?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, with no view, I fancy. Why not?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I'd rather,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"that connected me with the open

air."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Cecil, whatever do you mean?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The Sacred Lake!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why do you call it that?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I can't remember why. I suppose it comes out of some book. It's only a

puddle now, but you see that stream going through it? Well, a good deal

of water comes down after heavy rains, and can't get away at once, and

the pool becomes quite large and beautiful. Then Freddy used to bathe

there. He is very fond of it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Are you fond of it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I bathed

here, too, till I was found out. Then there was a row."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Who found you out?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Charlotte,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"She was stopping with us.

Charlotte--Charlotte."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Poor girl!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, I suppose we ought to be going,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy, I want to ask something of you that I have never asked before."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What, Cecil?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Hitherto never--not even that day on the lawn when you agreed to marry

me--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Up to now I have never kissed you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No--more you have,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then I ask you--may I now?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Of course, you may, Cecil. You might before. I can't run at you, you

know."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Emerson was the name, not Harris."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What name?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The old man's."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What old man?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That old man I told you about. The one Mr. Eager was so unkind to."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I cannot think

what people are doing,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"but it is extremely fortunate

for the children."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Does that very much matter?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, it has been such a nuisance--first he, then they--no one knowing

what they wanted, and every one so tiresome."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But they really are coming now,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I wrote to Miss

Teresa a few days ago--she was wondering how often the butcher called,

and my reply of once a month must have impressed her favourably. They

are coming. I heard from them this morning.



"I shall hate those Miss Alans!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Just because

they're old and silly one's expected to say 'How sweet!' I hate

their 'if'-ing and 'but'-ing and 'and'-ing. And poor Lucy--serve her

right--worn to a shadow."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, if they are coming--No, Minnie, not Saturn."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"If they are coming, Sir Harry will let them move

in before the twenty-ninth, and he will cross out the clause about

whitewashing the ceilings, because it made them nervous, and put in the

fair wear and tear one.--That doesn't count. I told you not Saturn."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Saturn's all right for bumble-puppy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Minnie, don't you listen to her."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Saturn doesn't bounce."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Saturn bounces enough."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, he doesn't."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well; he bounces better than the Beautiful White Devil."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hush, dear,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"But look at Lucy--complaining of Saturn, and all the time's got the

Beautiful White Devil in her hand, ready to plug it in. That's right,

Minnie, go for her--get her over the shins with the racquet--get her

over the shins!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"The name of this ball is Vittoria

Corombona, please."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wish the Miss Alans could see this,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Who are the Miss Alans?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They have taken Cissie Villa."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That wasn't the name--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Wasn't what name?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Alan wasn't the name of the people Sir Harry's let to."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nonsense, Freddy! You know nothing about it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Nonsense yourself! I've this minute seen him. He said to me: 'Ahem!

Honeychurch,'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"'ahem! ahem! I have at

last procured really dee-sire-rebel tenants.' I said, 'ooray, old boy!'

and slapped him on the back."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Exactly. The Miss Alans?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Rather not. More like Anderson."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, good gracious, there isn't going to be another muddle!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Do you notice, Lucy, I'm always right? I said

don't interfere with Cissie Villa. I'm always right. I'm quite uneasy at

being always right so often."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It's only another muddle of Freddy's. Freddy doesn't even know the name

of the people he pretends have taken it instead."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, I do. I've got it. Emerson."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What name?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Emerson. I'll bet you anything you like."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What a weathercock Sir Harry is,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I wish I had

never bothered over it at all."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Emerson, Freddy? Do you know what Emersons they are?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I don't know whether they're any Emersons,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I trust they are the right sort of person. All right, Lucy"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I see you looking down your nose and thinking your

mother's a snob. But there is a right sort and a wrong sort, and it's

affectation to pretend there isn't."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Emerson's a common enough name,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I was merely going to remark, Freddy, that I trusted they were no

relations of Emerson the philosopher, a most trying man. Pray, does that

satisfy you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, yes,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"And you will be satisfied, too, for they're

friends of Cecil; so"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"you and the other country

families will be able to call in perfect safety."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "CECIL?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't be rude, dear,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Lucy, don't screech.

It's a new bad habit you're getting into."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But has Cecil--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Friends of Cecil's,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"'and so really dee-sire-rebel. Ahem!

Honeychurch, I have just telegraphed to them.'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "screech"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"But Cecil's Emersons--they can't possibly be the

same ones--there is that--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"The Emersons who were at Florence, do you mean? No, I don't suppose it

will prove to be them. It is probably a long cry from them to friends

of Mr. Vyse's. Oh, Mrs. Honeychurch, the oddest people! The queerest

people! For our part we liked them, didn't we?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"There was a great scene over some violets. They picked violets and

filled all the vases in the room of these very Miss Alans who have

failed to come to Cissie Villa. Poor little ladies! So shocked and so

pleased. It used to be one of Miss Catharine's great stories. 'My dear

sister loves flowers,' it began. They found the whole room a mass of

blue--vases and jugs--and the story ends with 'So ungentlemanly and yet

so beautiful.' It is all very difficult. Yes, I always connect those

Florentine Emersons with violets."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Fiasco's done you this time,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"These particular Emersons consisted of a father and a son--the son

a goodly, if not a good young man; not a fool, I fancy, but very

immature--pessimism, et cetera. Our special joy was the father--such a

sentimental darling, and people declared he had murdered his wife."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Murdered his wife?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Lucy, don't desert us--go

on playing bumble-puppy. Really, the Pension Bertolini must have been

the oddest place. That's the second murderer I've heard of as being

there. Whatever was Charlotte doing to stop? By-the-by, we really must

ask Charlotte here some time."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, don't go!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I must go,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Don't be silly. You always overdo it

when you play."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Harris!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cecil!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hullo!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I was hoping you'd come. I heard you all

bear-gardening, but there's better fun up here. I, even I, have won a

great victory for the Comic Muse. George Meredith's right--the cause of

Comedy and the cause of Truth are really the same; and I, even I, have

found tenants for the distressful Cissie Villa. Don't be angry! Don't be

angry! You'll forgive me when you hear it all."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have heard,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Freddy has told us. Naughty Cecil! I suppose

I must forgive you. Just think of all the trouble I took for nothing!

Certainly the Miss Alans are a little tiresome, and I'd rather have nice

friends of yours. But you oughtn't to tease one so."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Friends of mine?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"But, Lucy, the whole joke is to come!

Come here."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Do you know where

I met these desirable tenants? In the National Gallery, when I was up to

see my mother last week."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What an odd place to meet people!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't quite

understand."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"In the Umbrian Room. Absolute strangers. They were admiring Luca

Signorelli--of course, quite stupidly. However, we got talking, and they

refreshed me not--a little. They had been to Italy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But, Cecil--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"In the course of conversation they said that they wanted a country

cottage--the father to live there, the son to run down for week-ends.

I thought, 'What a chance of scoring off Sir Harry!' and I took

their address and a London reference, found they weren't actual

blackguards--it was great sport--and wrote to him, making out--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cecil! No, it's not fair. I've probably met them before--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Perfectly fair. Anything is fair that punishes a snob. That old man

will do the neighbourhood a world of good. Sir Harry is too disgusting

with his 'decayed gentlewomen.' I meant to read him a lesson some time.

No, Lucy, the classes ought to mix, and before long you'll agree with

me. There ought to be intermarriage--all sorts of things. I believe in

democracy--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, you don't,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You don't know what the word means."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, you don't!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It isn't fair, Cecil. I blame you--I blame you very much indeed. You

had no business to undo my work about the Miss Alans, and make me look

ridiculous. You call it scoring off Sir Harry, but do you realize that

it is all at my expense? I consider it most disloyal of you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Temper!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cecil--Cecil darling,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "So you do love me, little thing?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Cecil, I do, I do! I don't know what I should do without you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "the flight to Rome,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Tunbridge Wells,



"September.



"Dearest Lucia,



"I have news of you at last! Miss Lavish has been bicycling in your

parts, but was not sure whether a call would be welcome. Puncturing

her tire near Summer Street, and it being mended while she sat very

woebegone in that pretty churchyard, she saw to her astonishment, a door

open opposite and the younger Emerson man come out. He said his father

had just taken the house. He SAID he did not know that you lived in the

neighbourhood (?). He never suggested giving Eleanor a cup of tea. Dear

Lucy, I am much worried, and I advise you to make a clean breast of his

past behaviour to your mother, Freddy, and Mr. Vyse, who will forbid him

to enter the house, etc. That was a great misfortune, and I dare say you

have told them already. Mr. Vyse is so sensitive. I remember how I used

to get on his nerves at Rome. I am very sorry about it all, and should

not feel easy unless I warned you.



"Believe me,



"Your anxious and loving cousin,



"Charlotte."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Beauchamp Mansions, S.W.



"Dear Charlotte,



"Many thanks for your warning. When Mr. Emerson forgot himself on the

mountain, you made me promise not to tell mother, because you said she

would blame you for not being always with me. I have kept that promise,

and cannot possibly tell her now. I have said both to her and Cecil

that I met the Emersons at Florence, and that they are respectable

people--which I do think--and the reason that he offered Miss Lavish no

tea was probably that he had none himself. She should have tried at the

Rectory. I cannot begin making a fuss at this stage. You must see that

it would be too absurd. If the Emersons heard I had complained of them,

they would think themselves of importance, which is exactly what they

are not. I like the old father, and look forward to seeing him again.

As for the son, I am sorry for him when we meet, rather than for myself.

They are known to Cecil, who is very well and spoke of you the other

day. We expect to be married in January.



"Miss Lavish cannot have told you much about me, for I am not at Windy

Corner at all, but here. Please do not put 'Private' outside your

envelope again. No one opens my letters.



"Yours affectionately,



"L. M. Honeychurch."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Emerson, not Harris"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Now some Beethoven"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Too much Schumann"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Make Lucy one of us,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy is becoming wonderful--wonderful."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Her music always was wonderful."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Yes, but she is purging off the Honeychurch taint, most excellent

Honeychurches, but you know what I mean. She is not always quoting

servants, or asking one how the pudding is made."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Italy has done it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It is just possible. Cecil, mind you marry her next January.

She is one of us already."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But her music!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"The style of her! How she kept to

Schumann when, like an idiot, I wanted Beethoven. Schumann was right for

this evening. Schumann was the thing. Do you know, mother, I shall have

our children educated just like Lucy. Bring them up among honest country

folks for freshness, send them to Italy for subtlety, and then--not

till then--let them come to London. I don't believe in these London

educations--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "At all events, not for women."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Make her one of us,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am so sorry, Mrs. Vyse--it is these dreams."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Bad dreams?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Just dreams."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You

should have heard us talking about you, dear. He admires you more than

ever. Dream of that."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Suppose we go and hinder those new people opposite for a little."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They might amuse you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I suggested we should hinder them,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"They are worth

it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hullo!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hullo!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I've brought some one to see you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I'll be down in a minute."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Are these people great readers?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Are they that

sort?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I fancy they know how to read--a rare accomplishment. What have they

got? Byron. Exactly. A Shropshire Lad. Never heard of it. The Way of

All Flesh. Never heard of it. Gibbon. Hullo! dear George reads German.

Um--um--Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and so we go on. Well, I suppose your

generation knows its own business, Honeychurch."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mr. Beebe, look at that,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mistrust all enterprises that require new clothes."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I know. Isn't it jolly? I like that. I'm certain that's the old man's

doing."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How very odd of him!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Surely you agree?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Pictures!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Giotto--they got that at Florence, I'll be bound."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The same as Lucy's got."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, by-the-by, did Miss Honeychurch enjoy London?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She came back yesterday."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I suppose she had a good time?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, very,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"She and Cecil are thicker

than ever."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That's good hearing."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wish I wasn't such a fool, Mr. Beebe."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Lucy used to be nearly as stupid as I am, but it'll be very different

now, mother thinks. She will read all kinds of books."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "So will you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Only medical books. Not books that you can talk about afterwards. Cecil

is teaching Lucy Italian, and he says her playing is wonderful. There

are all kinds of things in it that we have never noticed. Cecil says--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"What on earth are those people doing upstairs? Emerson--we think we'll

come another time."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Let me introduce Mr. Honeychurch, a neighbour."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"How d'ye do? Come and have

a bathe."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, all right,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "'How d'ye do? how d'ye do? Come and have a bathe,'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"That's the best conversational opening I've ever heard. But I'm afraid

it will only act between men. Can you picture a lady who has been

introduced to another lady by a third lady opening civilities with 'How

do you do? Come and have a bathe'? And yet you will tell me that the

sexes are equal."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I tell you that they shall be,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Good afternoon, Mr. Beebe. I tell you they shall

be comrades, and George thinks the same."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We are to raise ladies to our level?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The Garden of Eden,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"which you

place in the past, is really yet to come. We shall enter it when we no

longer despise our bodies."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"In this--not in other things--we men are ahead. We despise the body

less than women do. But not until we are comrades shall we enter the

garden."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I say, what about this bathe?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I believed in a return to Nature once. But how can we return to

Nature when we have never been with her? To-day, I believe that we must

discover Nature. After many conquests we shall attain simplicity. It is

our heritage."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Let me introduce Mr. Honeychurch, whose sister you will remember at

Florence."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"How do you do? Very glad to see you, and that you are taking George for

a bathe. Very glad to hear that your sister is going to marry. Marriage

is a duty. I am sure that she will be happy, for we know Mr. Vyse, too.

He has been most kind. He met us by chance in the National Gallery, and

arranged everything about this delightful house. Though I hope I have

not vexed Sir Harry Otway. I have met so few Liberal landowners, and

I was anxious to compare his attitude towards the game laws with the

Conservative attitude. Ah, this wind! You do well to bathe. Yours is a

glorious country, Honeychurch!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not a bit!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I must--that is to say, I have to--have

the pleasure of calling on you later on, my mother says, I hope."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"CALL, my lad? Who taught us that drawing-room twaddle? Call on your

grandmother! Listen to the wind among the pines! Yours is a glorious

country."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Mr. Emerson, he will call, I shall call; you or your son will return

our calls before ten days have elapsed. I trust that you have realized

about the ten days' interval. It does not count that I helped you with

the stair-eyes yesterday. It does not count that they are going to bathe

this afternoon."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Yes, go and bathe, George. Why do you dawdle talking? Bring them back

to tea. Bring back some milk, cakes, honey. The change will do you good.

George has been working very hard at his office. I can't believe he's

well."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you really want this bathe?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It is only a pond,

don't you know. I dare say you are used to something better."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes--I have said 'Yes' already."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"And what a coincidence that you should meet Mr. Vyse! Did you realize

that you would find all the Pension Bertolini down here?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I did not. Miss Lavish told me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"When I was a young man, I always meant to write a 'History of

Coincidence.'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Though, as a matter of fact, coincidences are much rarer than we

suppose. For example, it isn't purely coincidentally that you are here

now, when one comes to reflect."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It is. I have reflected. It is Fate. Everything is Fate. We are flung

together by Fate, drawn apart by Fate--flung together, drawn apart. The

twelve winds blow us--we settle nothing--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You have not reflected at all,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Let me give you

a useful tip, Emerson: attribute nothing to Fate. Don't say, 'I didn't

do this,' for you did it, ten to one. Now I'll cross-question you. Where

did you first meet Miss Honeychurch and myself?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Italy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"And where did you meet Mr. Vyse, who is going to marry Miss

Honeychurch?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "National Gallery."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Looking at Italian art. There you are, and yet you talk of coincidence

and Fate. You naturally seek out things Italian, and so do we and our

friends. This narrows the field immeasurably we meet again in it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is Fate that I am here,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"But you can call it

Italy if it makes you less unhappy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"And so for this and for other reasons my 'History of Coincidence' is

still to write."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"We are all so glad that you

have come."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Here we are!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, good!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In there's the pond. I wish it was bigger,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's distinctly successful, as ponds go,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No apologies

are necessary for the pond."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Aren't those masses of willow-herb splendid? I love willow-herb in

seed. What's the name of this aromatic plant?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"These abrupt changes of vegetation--this little spongeous tract of

water plants, and on either side of it all the growths are tough or

brittle--heather, bracken, hurts, pines. Very charming, very charming.



"Mr. Beebe, aren't you bathing?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Water's wonderful!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Water's water,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Apooshoo, apooshoo, apooshoo,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is it worth it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Hee-poof--I've swallowed a pollywog, Mr. Beebe, water's wonderful,

water's simply ripping."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Water's not so bad,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Water's wonderful. Mr. Beebe, do."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Apooshoo, kouf."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I may as well wash too"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Race you round it, then,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No. We are what matters. Without us shall no enterprise begin. To us

shall all flesh turn in the end."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A try! A try!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Socker rules,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Goal!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Goal!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Pass!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Take care my watch!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Take care my hat! No, that's enough, Freddy. Dress now. No, I say!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That'll do!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hi! Steady on! I see people coming you fellows!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hi! hi! LADIES!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Gracious alive!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Whoever were those

unfortunate people? Oh, dears, look away! And poor Mr. Beebe, too!

Whatever has happened?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Come this way immediately,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, poor Mr. Beebe! Was that his waistcoat we left in the path? Cecil,

Mr. Beebe's waistcoat--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "minded."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I fancy Mr. Beebe jumped back into the pond."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "This way, please, Mrs. Honeychurch, this way."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, I can't help it,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I can't

be trodden on, can I?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Good gracious me, dear; so it's you! What miserable management! Why not

have a comfortable bath at home, with hot and cold laid on?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Look here, mother, a fellow must wash, and a fellow's got to dry, and

if another fellow--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Dear, no doubt you're right as usual, but you are in no position to

argue. Come, Lucy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, look--don't look! Oh, poor Mr.

Beebe! How unfortunate again--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And me, I've swallowed one,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I've

swallowed a pollywog. It wriggleth in my tummy. I shall die--Emerson you

beast, you've got on my bags."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hush, dears,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"And do be sure you dry yourselves thoroughly first. All these

colds come of not drying thoroughly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mother, do come away,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh for goodness' sake, do come."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hullo!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hullo, Miss Honeychurch! Hullo!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Bow, Lucy; better bow. Whoever is it? I shall bow."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I will bow,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I will not shake hands with him.

That will be just the proper thing."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"is anything the matter

with Cecil?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, I don't think so, mother; Cecil's all right."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps he's tired."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Because otherwise"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "because otherwise I cannot account for him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do think Mrs. Butterworth is rather tiresome, if you mean that."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Cecil has told you to think so. You were devoted to her as a little

girl, and nothing will describe her goodness to you through the typhoid

fever. No--it is just the same thing everywhere."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Let me just put your bonnet away, may I?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Surely he could answer her civilly for one half-hour?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Cecil has a very high standard for people,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It's part of his ideals--it is really that that makes

him sometimes seem--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, rubbish! If high ideals make a young man rude, the sooner he gets

rid of them the better,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Now, mother! I've seen you cross with Mrs. Butterworth yourself!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Not in that way. At times I could wring her neck. But not in that way.

No. It is the same with Cecil all over."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"By-the-by--I never told you. I had a letter from Charlotte while I was

away in London."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Since Cecil came back from London, nothing appears to please him.

Whenever I speak he winces;--I see him, Lucy; it is useless to

contradict me. No doubt I am neither artistic nor literary nor

intellectual nor musical, but I cannot help the drawing-room furniture;

your father bought it and we must put up with it, will Cecil kindly

remember."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I--I see what you mean, and certainly Cecil oughtn't to. But he does

not mean to be uncivil--he once explained--it is the things that upset

him--he is easily upset by ugly things--he is not uncivil to PEOPLE."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is it a thing or a person when Freddy sings?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You can't expect a really musical person to enjoy comic songs as we

do."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Then why didn't he leave the room? Why sit wriggling and sneering and

spoiling everyone's pleasure?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We mustn't be unjust to people,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Go and dress, dear; you'll be late."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "All right, mother--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't say 'All right' and stop. Go."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, dear, what shall I do, what shall I do?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I say, those are topping people."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"My dear baby, how tiresome you've been! You have no business to take

them bathing in the Sacred it's much too public. It was all right for

you but most awkward for every one else. Do be more careful. You forget

the place is growing half suburban."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I say, is anything on to-morrow week?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not that I know of."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then I want to ask the Emersons up to Sunday tennis."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, I wouldn't do that, Freddy, I wouldn't do that with all this

muddle."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"What's wrong with the court? They won't mind a bump or two, and I've

ordered new balls."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I meant it's better not. I really mean it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Lucy, what a noise you're making! I

have something to say to you. Did you say you had had a letter from

Charlotte?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes. I really can't stop. I must dress too."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How's Charlotte?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "All right."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You've a bad habit of hurrying away in the middle of one's sentences.

Did Charlotte mention her boiler?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Her WHAT?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Don't you remember that her boiler was to be had out in October, and

her bath cistern cleaned out, and all kinds of terrible to-doings?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I can't remember all Charlotte's worries,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I shall

have enough of my own, now that you are not pleased with Cecil."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Come

here, old lady--thank you for putting away my bonnet--kiss me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy, what's Emerson like?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I saw him in Florence,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is he the clever sort, or is he a decent chap?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ask Cecil; it is Cecil who brought him here."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is the clever sort, like myself,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How well did you know them at the Bertolini?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, very slightly. I mean, Charlotte knew them even less than I did."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Oh, that reminds me--you never told me what Charlotte said in her

letter."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "One thing and another,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Among other things, that an awful

friend of hers had been bicycling through Summer Street, wondered if

she'd come up and see us, and mercifully didn't."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy, I do call the way you talk unkind."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She was a novelist,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"If books must be written, let them be

written by men"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "This year, next year, now, never,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have been thinking, Lucy, of that letter of Charlotte's. How is she?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I tore the thing up."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Didn't she say how she was? How does she sound? Cheerful?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, yes I suppose so--no--not very cheerful, I suppose."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Then, depend upon it, it IS the boiler. I know myself how water preys

upon one's mind. I would rather anything else--even a misfortune with

the meat."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "So would I,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And I have been thinking,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"surely we could

squeeze Charlotte in here next week, and give her a nice holiday while

plumbers at Tunbridge Wells finish. I have not seen poor Charlotte for

so long."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mother, no!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It's impossible. We can't have Charlotte on

the top of the other things; we're squeezed to death as it is. Freddy's

got a friend coming Tuesday, there's Cecil, and you've promised to take

in Minnie Beebe because of the diphtheria scare. It simply can't be

done."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nonsense! It can."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If Minnie sleeps in the bath. Not otherwise."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Minnie can sleep with you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I won't have her."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then, if you're so selfish, Mr. Floyd must share a room with Freddy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Miss Bartlett, Miss Bartlett, Miss Bartlett,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's impossible,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't want to make difficulties,

but it really isn't fair on the maids to fill up the house so."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The truth is, dear, you don't like Charlotte."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No, I don't. And no more does Cecil. She gets on our nerves. You

haven't seen her lately, and don't realize how tiresome she can be,

though so good. So please, mother, don't worry us this last summer; but

spoil us by not asking her to come."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hear, hear!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"This isn't very kind of

you two. You have each other and all these woods to walk in, so full of

beautiful things; and poor Charlotte has only the water turned off and

plumbers. You are young, dears, and however clever young people are, and

however many books they read, they will never guess what it feels like

to grow old."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I must say Cousin Charlotte was very kind to me that year I called on

my bike,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"She thanked me for coming till I felt like

such a fool, and fussed round no end to get an egg boiled for my tea

just right."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I know, dear. She is kind to every one, and yet Lucy makes this

difficulty when we try to give her some little return."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I

can't help it, mother. I don't like Charlotte. I admit it's horrid of

me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "From your own account, you told her as much."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, she would leave Florence so stupidly. She flurried--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I suppose Miss Bartlett must come, since she boils eggs so well,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I didn't mean the egg was WELL boiled,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"because in

point of fact she forgot to take it off, and as a matter of fact I don't

care for eggs. I only meant how jolly kind she seemed."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"May me and Lucy get down from

our chairs?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"We don't want no

dessert."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "things that came out of nothing and meant she didn't know what."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"She loves young

Emerson."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "nerves"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A nice fellow,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"He will work off his

crudities in time. I rather mistrust young men who slip into life

gracefully."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He seems in better spirits. He laughs more."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is waking up."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I shall never forgive myself,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I have upset everything. Bursting in on young people! But I insist on

paying for my cab up. Grant that, at any rate."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Our visitors never do such dreadful things,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Just what I've been trying to convince

Cousin Charlotte of, Lucy, for the last half hour."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do not feel myself an ordinary visitor,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"All right, if you'd really rather. Five shillings, and I gave a bob to

the driver."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"But who

am I to give the sovereign to?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Let's leave it all till mother comes back,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No, dear; your mother may take quite a long drive now that she is not

hampered with me. We all have our little foibles, and mine is the prompt

settling of accounts."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Please--please--I know I am a sad spoilsport, but it would make me

wretched. I should practically be robbing the one who lost."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Freddy owes me fifteen shillings,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"So it will work

out right if you give the pound to me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Fifteen shillings,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"How is that, Mr.

Vyse?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Because, don't you see, Freddy paid your cab. Give me the pound, and we

shall avoid this deplorable gambling."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But I don't see that!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't see why Mr. Vyse is to have the

quid."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Because of the fifteen shillings and the five,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Fifteen shillings and five shillings make one pound, you see."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But I don't see--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No, thank you. I'm done. I don't see why--Freddy, don't poke me. Miss

Honeychurch, your brother's hurting me. Ow! What about Mr. Floyd's

ten shillings? Ow! No, I don't see and I never shall see why Miss

What's-her-name shouldn't pay that bob for the driver."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I had forgotten the driver,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Thank you,

dear, for reminding me. A shilling was it? Can any one give me change

for half a crown?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I'll get it,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Cecil, give me that sovereign. No, give me up that sovereign. I'll get

Euphemia to change it, and we'll start the whole thing again from the

beginning."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy--Lucy--what a nuisance I am!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Have you told him about him yet?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, I haven't,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Let me see--a

sovereign's worth of silver."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, I haven't told Cecil or any one,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I promised you I shouldn't. Here is your money--all shillings, except

two half-crowns. Would you count it? You can settle your debt nicely

now."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How dreadful!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"how more than dreadful, if Mr. Vyse

should come to hear of it from some other source."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, no, Charlotte,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"George Emerson

is all right, and what other source is there?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"For instance, the driver. I saw him looking

through the bushes at you, remember he had a violet between his teeth."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"We shall get the silly affair on our nerves

if we aren't careful. How could a Florentine cab-driver ever get hold of

Cecil?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We must think of every possibility."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, it's all right."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Or perhaps old Mr. Emerson knows. In fact, he is certain to know."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I don't care if he does. I was grateful to you for your letter, but

even if the news does get round, I think I can trust Cecil to laugh at

it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To contradict it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, to laugh at it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Very well, dear, you know best. Perhaps gentlemen are different to what

they were when I was young. Ladies are certainly different."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Now, Charlotte!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"You kind, anxious thing.

What WOULD you have me do? First you say 'Don't tell'; and then you say,

'Tell'. Which is it to be? Quick!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"I am no match for you in conversation, dearest. I

blush when I think how I interfered at Florence, and you so well able

to look after yourself, and so much cleverer in all ways than I am. You

will never forgive me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Shall we go out, then. They will smash all the china if we don't."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Dear, one moment--we may not have this chance for a chat again. Have

you seen the young one yet?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, I have."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What happened?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We met at the Rectory."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What line is he taking up?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"No line. He talked about Italy, like any other person. It is really all

right. What advantage would he get from being a cad, to put it bluntly?

I do wish I could make you see it my way. He really won't be any

nuisance, Charlotte."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Once a cad, always a cad. That is my poor opinion."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Cecil said one day--and I thought it so profound--that

there are two kinds of cads--the conscious and the subconscious."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Once a cad, always a cad,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"What I mean by subconscious is that Emerson lost his head. I fell into

all those violets, and he was silly and surprised. I don't think we

ought to blame him very much. It makes such a difference when you see a

person with beautiful things behind him unexpectedly. It really does;

it makes an enormous difference, and he lost his head: he doesn't admire

me, or any of that nonsense, one straw. Freddy rather likes him, and

has asked him up here on Sunday, so you can judge for yourself. He has

improved; he doesn't always look as if he's going to burst into

tears. He is a clerk in the General Manager's office at one of the big

railways--not a porter! and runs down to his father for week-ends. Papa

was to do with journalism, but is rheumatic and has retired. There!

Now for the garden."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Suppose we

don't talk about this silly Italian business any more. We want you to

have a nice restful visit at Windy Corner, with no worriting."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"The men say they won't

go"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, I don't blame them"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "need she go?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Tell

her, no nonsense"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Anne! Mary! Hook me behind!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Dearest Lucia, may I

trespass upon you for a pin?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Lucy! Lucy! What's that book? Who's been taking a book out of the shelf

and leaving it about to spoil?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's only the library book that Cecil's been reading."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But pick it up, and don't stand idling there like a flamingo."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What! you aren't forgetting your Italy already?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lucy--have you a sixpence for Minnie and a shilling for yourself?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"It's a special collection--I forget what for. I do beg, no vulgar

clinking in the plate with halfpennies; see that Minnie has a nice

bright sixpence. Where is the child? Minnie! That book's all warped.

(Gracious, how plain you look!) Put it under the Atlas to press.

Minnie!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Mrs. Honeychurch--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Minnie, don't be late. Here comes the horse"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Where's Charlotte? Run up and hurry her. Why is she

so long? She had nothing to do. She never brings anything but blouses.

Poor Charlotte--How I do detest blouses! Minnie!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Dear Marian, I am very sorry, but I have no small change--nothing but

sovereigns and half crowns. Could any one give me--"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Yes, easily. Jump in. Gracious me, how smart you look! What a lovely

frock! You put us all to shame."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"If I did not wear my best rags and tatters now, when should I wear

them?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Good-bye! Be good!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown
